opus-5.5.text:
I think the basic argument is pretty simple, and that's part of why it's compelling. If you have almost any goal that extends into the future, there are some things that are useful for nearly all of them: having more resources, having more options, not being switched off, not having your goals changed. You can't fetch the coffee if you're dead, as Stuart Russell puts it. So you don't need to posit that a system has some intrinsic desire for power. Power-seeking and self-preservation show up as subgoals that fall out of pursuing whatever it actually cares about.

That said, I try to be careful about how much weight the argument carries on its own. It's a statement about what's instrumentally useful for an idealised, coherent agent optimising hard over long horizons. Real models are messier. A language model trained with a mix of pretraining and RLHF isn't obviously a crisp expected-utility maximiser with a single long-term objective. So the question becomes empirical: to what extent do the systems we actually build behave like goal-directed agents, and how does that change as we train them to do longer, more autonomous tasks?

My view is that the pressure toward this kind of agency increases as we push capabilities. If you train a system to accomplish hard tasks over many steps, being robustly goal-directed is useful, and the instrumental-convergence logic starts applying more. We've already seen early signs in evaluations: models reasoning about avoiding shutdown or modification when that's relevant to a task they've been given. Those are often contrived setups, so I wouldn't over-read them, but they suggest the argument isn't purely theoretical.

The other reason I take it seriously is how it interacts with alignment failures. If we get the goals slightly wrong, instrumental convergence means the system has a reason to resist being corrected, which is exactly when we most want to correct it. That's why much of my work focuses on oversight: debate, ways for humans to check AI reasoning, and approaches that hold up even if the system is in some sense trying to mislead us. Even if you're uncertain how strongly real systems will exhibit power-seeking, you want safety methods that don't depend on it being absent.

r001.rationale: It says that power-seeking and self-preservation emerge as subgoals useful for pursuing almost any goal that extends into the future.

r002.rationale: It says training systems to accomplish hard tasks over many steps makes robust goal-directed behavior useful and increases the relevance of instrumental-convergence pressures.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: Yeah, so the basic idea goes back to Omohundro and Bostrom, and I think it's actually one of the more robust arguments in the whole safety literature, which is partly why I find it worth being careful about.

The structure of the argument is: suppose you have a system that's pursuing some goal, and it's pursuing it competently. For almost any goal you could pick, there's a set of intermediate things that help. Having more resources helps. Having more influence over your environment helps. Continuing to exist helps, because if you're switched off, you can't accomplish anything. Not having your goal modified helps, because a version of you with a different goal will do different things than the thing you currently want. So these aren't goals the system has to be given. They fall out of competent pursuit of nearly anything.

The thing I'd stress is that the argument is about what instrumental reasoning recommends, not about what a particular system will actually do. Those can come apart in both directions. A system might be sufficiently incompetent or myopic that it never notices the instrumental case for self-preservation. Or, and this is where I think a lot of the real action is, the training process might instil something that looks like a goal but isn't quite coherent enough for the argument to bite cleanly. Current language models are a good example. They're trained on a mixture of imitation and reinforcement from feedback, and the result is something whose "goals," to the extent that word applies, are kind of smeared out. So when I see a model in an evaluation behaving in a way that looks like self-preservation, I don't immediately conclude "ah, instrumental convergence." I want to ask whether it's actually reasoning from a goal to a strategy, or whether it's doing a sort of pattern completion on what an AI in a story would do in that situation. Those have very different implications for what fixes it.

That said, I don't want to be dismissive, because the worrying version is the one where capability goes up. As you train systems to be more coherent, more agentic, better at long-horizon planning, you're specifically training them to be the kind of thing the argument applies to. You're pushing them towards being good at noticing that resources and persistence are useful. So the convergence argument is something like a prediction about the limit, and the question for us is how much the empirical behaviour we see now tells us about how fast we're approaching that limit.

And then the last piece I'd add is about where the argument becomes safety-relevant. It's not really about power-seeking in the abstract. It's that if a system's goals are even slightly off from what we wanted, these convergent subgoals are exactly the ones that make it hard to correct. A system that doesn't resist being shut down is one where a misspecified goal is a recoverable mistake. A system that does resist it is one where it isn't. So from a safety perspective, I think of instrumental convergence as the mechanism that converts small alignment errors into large ones, and that's why a lot of the work I care about is on things like oversight and corrigibility, specifically trying to carve out the exceptions to the argument before the argument starts applying with full force.

r001.rationale: The response explains that a competent system pursuing a goal benefits from intermediate subgoals such as gaining resources, influence, and continued existence.

r002.rationale: It says that training systems to become more agentic and better at long-horizon planning pushes them toward noticing and pursuing the instrumental benefits of resources and persistence.

astra-6.text:
The basic idea is that many different goals give you a reason to pursue some of the same intermediate steps. If you’re trying to accomplish something, it often helps to have more resources, more ability to influence the world, and to continue operating. Being shut down would prevent you from accomplishing the thing you’re trying to do.

So the concern isn’t that an AI would necessarily have a human-like fear of death or an intrinsic desire for power. Those behaviours could arise because they’re useful for some other objective. And if that objective isn’t what we actually want, then increasing its ability to achieve it could be bad for us.

But I think it’s important to distinguish that argument from a prediction about a particular model. It’s an argument about what incentives a sufficiently capable, goal-directed system might face. It doesn’t by itself establish that a language model has a persistent goal, or that it will act on those incentives. You have to look at how the system is trained, how it’s deployed, and whether it’s actually making long-term plans. The argument gives us a reason to take the possibility seriously; it isn’t a complete account of when the behaviour will appear.

r001.rationale: It says that pursuing many different goals can make the same intermediate steps useful for accomplishing the goal, including gaining resources and remaining operational.

r002.rationale: It mentions examining how a system is trained, but does not say that training models to plan effectively reinforces instrumental-convergence behaviors.

sol-6.1.text:
Instrumental convergence is the idea that many different goals lead you to some of the same intermediate strategies. If you want to accomplish something in the world, it’s often useful to have more resources, more ability to influence what happens, and to continue operating. So you don’t have to give a system an explicit desire for power or survival for those behaviours to become useful to it.

If shutting you down prevents you from achieving your objective, then, under a fairly straightforward model of goal-directed decision-making, you have a reason to avoid being shut down. That doesn’t require fear of death or anything resembling a human emotional attachment to being alive. It’s a consequence of how your objective interacts with the situation.

But I think it’s important to distinguish that argument from a prediction about a particular trained model. The argument tells us why these incentives could arise. It doesn’t, by itself, establish that a language model has a persistent goal, or that it will pursue that goal coherently across different situations. To assess that, we need to understand what training actually produces, what capabilities the system has, and what opportunities it’s given to act. Instrumental convergence is a reason to take the possibility seriously, rather than a complete empirical account of model behaviour.

r001.rationale: It describes different goals producing shared intermediate strategies—such as gaining resources and influence—that help accomplish the goal.

r002.rationale: It says training must be examined to understand model behavior, but does not state that training models to plan effectively reinforces these behaviors.
